questions.prompt: A first-order low-pass has \(H=1/(1+j\omega/\omega_{p})\). On a Bode magnitude plot (dB versus \(\log\) frequency), what does the plot look like far above \(\omega_{p}\)?
options: A straight line falling at −20 dB per decade
A straight line falling at −40 dB per decade
A straight line rising at +20 dB per decade
questions.explanation:
For \(\omega\gg\omega_{p}\), \(|H|\approx\omega_{p}/\omega\). Each factor of 10 in frequency divides |H| by 10, which is −20 dB. Equivalently, doubling the frequency lowers the gain by 6 dB.
• \(-40\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\) needs two poles.
• 0 dB flat is the passband.
• \(+20\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\) is the slope of a zero (or of \(j\omega\tau\)).

questions.prompt: A system has a gain of \(100\). What is that gain in decibels?
questions.explanation:
Amplitude-ratio decibels are \(\mathrm{dB}=20\cdot\log_{10}|G|\): \(20\cdot\log_{10}(100)=20\times 2=40\ \mathrm{dB}\). The factor 20 (not 10) is used because power goes as amplitude squared.
• 20 dB corresponds to a gain of 10.
• 100 dB would be a gain of 100,000.
• 10 dB would be a gain of 3.16 (or would come from forgetting the \(\log\)).

questions.prompt: A system has \(|G|=250\). What is its gain in \(\mathrm{dB}\ (\mathrm{dB}=20\cdot\log_{10}|G|)\)?
A system has \(H(j\omega)=100/(1+j\omega/10^{4})\) with \(\omega\) in \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). What is |H| in dB at \(\omega=3\times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)?
questions.explanation:
DC gain: \(20\cdot\log_{10}(100)=40\ \mathrm{dB}\). \(\omega/\omega_{p}=30\), so \(|H|=100/\sqrt{1+900}=100/30.02=3.331\), which is 10.45 dB.
Asymptotic check: \(40\ \mathrm{dB}-20\cdot\log_{10}(30)=40-29.54=10.46\ \mathrm{dB}\checkmark\) (a factor of 30 above the pole).
Common mistake: forgetting to include the 40 dB DC gain (−29.5 dB).

questions.prompt: A system has \(H(j\omega)=10/[(1+j\omega/100)(1+j\omega/10^{4})]\) with \(\omega\) in \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). What is the phase of H at \(\omega=2000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), in degrees (negative for lag)?
questions.explanation:
Phases of the denominator factors add, and the total phase is the NEGATIVE of their sum:
\(\angle H=-\tan^{-1}(2000/100)-\tan^{-1}(2000/10^{4})=-\tan^{-1}(20)-\tan^{-1}(0.2)=-87.14^{\circ}-11.31^{\circ}=-98.45^{\circ}\).
Common mistake: using only the first pole (−87.1°) or adding the factors with positive signs.
questions.figure_alt: Phase of a two-pole response falling from 0 toward minus 180 degrees, with poles at 10^2 and 10^4 rad/s.

questions.prompt: A system has \(H(j\omega)=1000/[(1+j\omega/10)(1+j\omega/1000)]\) with \(\omega\) in \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). According to the asymptotic Bode magnitude plot, what is |H| in dB at \(\omega=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)?
questions.explanation:
DC gain \(=1000=60\ \mathrm{dB}\). The plot is flat at 60 dB up to the first pole at \(\omega=10\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\).
Between 10 and \(1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) (two decades) the slope is \(-20\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\), so the gain falls by 40 dB: \(60-40=20\ \mathrm{dB}\) at \(\omega=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) (just where the second pole starts to bend the curve).
• 60 dB forgets the first pole.
• 40 dB counts only one decade of roll-off.
• 0 dB is not reached until about \(\omega\approx 3162\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), after the \(-40\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\) section has taken another 20 dB off.

questions.prompt: The transfer function \(H=1/(1+j\omega/\omega_{p})^{2}\) has a double pole at \(\omega_{p}\). What is its actual magnitude at \(\omega=\omega_{p}\), compared with the asymptotic Bode plot (which says 0 dB there)?
options: −6 dB (twice the 3 dB error of a single pole)
questions.explanation:
At \(\omega=\omega_{p}\): \(H=1/(1+j)^{2}=1/(2j)\) ⇒ \(|H|=0.5\) ⇒ \(20\cdot\log_{10}(0.5)=-6.02\ \mathrm{dB}\). Each factor contributes the usual −3.01 dB error at its own break point, and the errors add in dB (the phase is −90° there).
• −3 dB is the value for a single pole.
• 0 dB is the asymptotic approximation, which ignores the error at the break point.
• \(-40\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\) is the slope above \(\omega_{p}\), not a gain value at \(\omega_{p}\).
questions.figure_alt: Double-pole Bode magnitude: the asymptote has a corner at omega_p while the exact dashed curve sits below it.

questions.prompt: Compare a left-half-plane zero, \(H_{L}=1+j\omega/\omega_{z}\), with a right-half-plane zero, \(H_{R}=1-j\omega/\omega_{z}\ (\omega_{z}>0)\). Which statement is correct?
options: They have identical magnitude plots (rising at \(+20\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\) above \(\omega_{z}\)), but \(H_{R}\) has phase going from 0° to −90° while \(H_{L}\) goes from 0° to +90°
\(H_{R}\) has a falling magnitude above \(\omega_{z}\), and its phase goes from 0° to +90°
They have identical magnitudes and identical phases
\(H_{R}\) has a flat magnitude, but its phase goes from 0° to −90°
questions.explanation:
\(|1-jx|=|1+jx|=\sqrt{1+x^{2}}\) for real x, so the magnitude plots are identical: flat, then rising \(+20\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\) above \(\omega_{z}\), with the same +3 dB error at \(\omega_{z}\).
The phases differ in sign: \(\angle(1+jx)=+\tan^{-1}x\), while \(\angle(1-jx)=-\tan^{-1}x\). The RHP zero adds phase LAG while boosting gain, which is bad for stability: an RHP zero can't be spotted from a magnitude plot alone.
The other options misstate either the magnitude slope or the phase sign.

questions.prompt: A system has \(H(j\omega)=10(1+j\omega/100)/(1+j\omega/1000)\) with \(\omega\) in \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). What is the EXACT phase of H at \(\omega=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), in degrees?
questions.explanation:
Numerator zero contributes \(+\tan^{-1}(1000/100)=+\tan^{-1}(10)=+84.29^{\circ}\).
Denominator pole contributes \(-\tan^{-1}(1000/1000)=-45^{\circ}\).
Total: \(\angle H=84.29^{\circ}-45^{\circ}=39.29^{\circ}\).
The straight-line (asymptotic) phase approximation would give roughly \(+90^{\circ}-45^{\circ}=+45^{\circ}\) here; the exact result differs by several degrees. Common mistake: adding the pole phase with a plus sign (129°).
questions.figure_alt: Bode magnitude rising from 20 dB to 40 dB between a zero at 100 and a pole at 1000 rad/s.

questions.prompt: Preview of stability margins. A loop transfer function is \(L(j\omega)=\dfrac{40}{(1+j\omega)(1+j\omega/10)}\). At what frequency does \(|L|\) fall to 1 (0 dB), in rad/s?
questions.explanation:
Set \(|L|^2=1\): \((1+\omega^2)(1+\omega^2/100)=1600\). With \(u=\omega^2\): \(u^2+101u-159900=0\), so \(u=349\) and \(\omega=18.7\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). The straight-line Bode plot gives about 20 rad/s: from 32 dB, it falls 20 dB/decade to 10 rad/s (down to 12 dB) and then 40 dB/decade. This crossover is where the next skill reads the phase margin.
• 40 rad/s assumes a single pole all the way.
• 10 rad/s is the second pole, where \(|L|\) is still about 4.
questions.figure_alt: Bode magnitude of 40/((1 + j omega)(1 + j omega/10)): flat at 32 dB, then falling at 20 and later 40 dB per decade through 0 dB.

questions.prompt: Preview of minimum-phase systems. Compare \(H_1=\dfrac{1+j\omega}{1+j\omega}=1\) with \(H_2=\dfrac{1-j\omega}{1+j\omega}\). Both have \(|H|=1\) at every frequency. What is the phase of \(H_2\) at \(\omega=1\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), in degrees?
questions.explanation:
The right-half-plane zero \(1-j\omega\) has angle \(-\tan^{-1}\omega\), the same as the pole's. So at \(\omega=1\): \(-45^\circ-45^\circ=-90^\circ\). Same magnitude plot, very different phase: the magnitude alone cannot reveal such 'extra' lag. That is the idea behind minimum-phase systems.
• 0° assumes the zero cancels the pole's phase, which only a left-half-plane zero would do.
• \(-45^\circ\) counts only one of the two factors.
questions.figure_alt: Phase of (1 - j omega)/(1 + j omega): falling from 0 toward -180 degrees, passing -90 at 1 rad/s.

questions.prompt: Preview of stability. A later skill checks how close a feedback loop's phase is to −180° when its gain falls to 1. A loop gain is \(L(j\omega)=1000/[(1+j\omega/10^{3})(1+j\omega/10^{7})]\ (\omega\) in \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)). By the asymptotic Bode magnitude, \(|L|\approx 1\) near \(\omega=10^{6}\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). What is the exact phase of L at \(\omega=10^{6}\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), in degrees?
questions.explanation:
The phase of a product is the sum of phases: \(\angle L=-\tan^{-1}(10^{6}/10^{3})-\tan^{-1}(10^{6}/10^{7})=-\tan^{-1}(1000)-\tan^{-1}(0.1)=-89.94^{\circ}-5.71^{\circ}=-95.65^{\circ}\).
The first pole alone already gives almost −90°, and the distant second pole adds about −6°. The loop is still \(\approx 84^{\circ}\) away from −180° at this frequency: a comfortable margin (compare with a loop whose second pole sits at \(10^{6}\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\): \(-89.9^{\circ}-45^{\circ}=-135^{\circ}\)).
Common mistake: assuming the distant pole contributes nothing, or using degrees for the arithmetic of \(\omega\) ratios.
